content.overview: HTTP methods communicate intent. GET reads, POST creates/processes, PUT replaces, PATCH partially updates, and DELETE removes. The important skill is choosing semantics that make an API predictable and safe to use.
content.diagram: Client → method + URL + headers/body → server → status + headers/body
content.example: A task API might use GET /tasks to list, POST /tasks to create, PATCH /tasks/:id to rename, and DELETE /tasks/:id to remove.
content.commonMistakes: GET should not mutate state; validate request bodies; do not treat every request as POST.

content.overview: Status codes tell the client what happened at a protocol level. 2xx means success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client/request problems, and 5xx server-side failures. Consistent codes make clients, logs and debugging easier.
content.diagram: Request → server decision → 2xx / 3xx / 4xx / 5xx → client behavior
content.example: Return 201 after creating a resource, 400 for malformed input, 401 when authentication is missing, 403 when authenticated but forbidden, and 404 when the resource does not exist.
content.commonMistakes: Do not return 200 for every outcome; 401 and 403 are different; avoid leaking internal errors in 5xx responses.

content.overview: A closure happens when a function retains access to variables from its lexical scope after that outer scope has returned. Closures are useful for private state, factories and callbacks.

content.commonMistakes: Be careful with stale captured values and long-lived closures that retain large objects.

content.overview: A Promise represents the eventual result of asynchronous work. It can be pending, fulfilled, or rejected. Promise composition lets you sequence, parallelize and handle asynchronous operations without deeply nested callbacks.
content.diagram: start async work → pending → fulfilled value OR rejected error

content.commonMistakes: Do not forget rejection handling; do not use sequential awaits when operations are independent and latency matters.

content.overview: async/await is syntax for consuming Promises with code that reads like synchronous control flow. It does not make work synchronous; it makes asynchronous control flow easier to structure.
content.diagram: async function → await Promise → resume on fulfillment / throw on rejection

content.overview: JavaScript uses a call stack plus queues to coordinate asynchronous callbacks. Synchronous work runs first; microtasks such as Promise callbacks are processed before the next macrotask such as a timer callback.
content.diagram: call stack → async API → task queues → microtasks → next macrotask
content.example: After a synchronous log, a Promise.then callback runs before a setTimeout callback scheduled for the same turn.
content.commonMistakes: Do not say JavaScript is simply “single threaded so nothing is asynchronous”; the runtime delegates work and schedules callbacks.

content.overview: Passwords should be stored as slow, salted password hashes rather than plaintext or reversible encryption. A password verifier recomputes the derived value and compares it safely.
content.diagram: password → salted slow KDF → stored hash → later verification
content.example: Store a PBKDF2, bcrypt or Argon2 result with its salt and parameters, then verify during login.
content.commonMistakes: Never log passwords, never store plaintext, and do not use a fast general hash such as plain SHA-256 for password storage.

content.overview: Precision measures how many predicted positives are actually positive: TP/(TP+FP). It matters when false positives are costly.
